sections.h2: How does selling a house work in Maryland?
sections.html:
Selling a house in Maryland is a county-level process wrapped in state law. The state sets the rules for taxes, foreclosure, probate and landlord cases, but your county government, your county's Circuit Court and the local tax collector handle most of the paperwork. Knowing which office does what saves a lot of phone calls.

Maryland has 23 counties and one independent city, Baltimore, which works as a county equivalent for most purposes. Many towns bill their own property tax on top of the county bill. If your house is in a town such as Gaithersburg, Frederick or Annapolis, check whether the city sends a separate tax statement before you set a closing date.

A cash sale as-is means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and does not ask you to fix, paint or clean. You still need clear title, a paid-up tax account and a deed that can be recorded, so those items drive the timeline more than the condition of the house does.

sections.h2: Who do you call about property taxes when you sell?
sections.html:
Call the county or Baltimore City tax collector for the balance, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) for the assessed value. Maryland splits those jobs. SDAT determines the taxable assessment, while each county and Baltimore City maintains the tax accounts for real property inside its borders.

The calendar is fixed by the state. Property taxes are due without interest as of July 1 and become overdue on the following October 1. Owners of a principal residence may pay in two installments, due September 30 and December 31. Any unpaid tax is a lien on the property until it is paid, so a seller with a past-due bill usually pays it from proceeds at closing.

sections.h2: What happens if the taxes on my Maryland house go to tax sale?
sections.html:
A Maryland tax sale sells the debt, not the house. After an auction the homeowner still owns the property and keeps possession. The buyer gets a tax lien certificate and a right to foreclose if the debt is not paid in time.

The process runs on a schedule the county must follow:

  • The collector mails a notice at least 30 days before the property is first advertised in a newspaper.
  • The listing then runs once a week for four weeks, naming the owner and the amount owed.
  • About six months after the sale the buyer receives a certificate of sale.
  • Six months after the sale, or nine months for an owner-occupied residence, the buyer may file in Circuit Court to foreclose the right of redemption.

The owner can redeem at any point until a court finally forecloses that right, and the cost rises the longer the wait. Selling the house before a foreclosure judgment, and paying the certificate from the proceeds, is one way owners resolve it. Our Maryland tax sale guide covers the options in more detail.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in Maryland?
sections.html:
Maryland foreclosure goes through the Circuit Court in the county where the house sits, and there are several built-in pauses. A lender sends a Notice of Intent to Foreclose, usually about 45 days after default, and may file the court action 90 days after default. The notice has to arrive at least 45 days before the filing.

Owners who live in the house have a one-time chance to request foreclosure mediation. The request is due within 25 days of receiving the lender's final affidavit form and carries a $50 fee that a judge may waive. Investment and other non-owner-occupied properties are not eligible for mediation. If no mediation is requested, the lender may sell at public auction once 45 days have passed after the owner was served.

  • The lender must publish the sale notice in a local newspaper for at least three weeks in a row.
  • The owner must get written notice of the sale date at least 10 days ahead.
  • The owner can stop the sale by paying everything due up to one business day before it.

A sale before the auction date can end the case if it pays off the loan.

sections.h2: What should heirs know about selling an inherited house in Maryland?
sections.html:
Start with the Register of Wills in the jurisdiction where the person lived at death. Maryland law says anyone holding a document that looks like a will must file it promptly with that office, even if no one plans to probate it. Assets in the decedent's name alone are called probate assets, and they must be reported there.

The size of the estate decides the path. When probate assets total $50,000 or less, the estate can open as a small estate, which has fewer requirements and no required fee to the Register of Wills for estates opened since October 1, 2022. The limit is $100,000 if the surviving spouse is the only heir. Larger estates go through regular administration, and a personal representative has authority to sell real estate only after being appointed.

Taxes, insurance and utilities keep running on a vacant house while the estate is open. Our Maryland probate guide and estate and inheritance tax page explain who owes what, and the transfer on death deed page covers the newer deed option.

sections.h2: Who pays transfer tax and closing costs on a Maryland sale?
sections.html:
Maryland's default rule is a 50/50 split of recordation tax and any state or local transfer tax between buyer and seller, unless the contract says otherwise. The state transfer tax is 0.5 percent of the consideration, and local taxes add to it.

There is an important exception. When the buyer is a first-time Maryland buyer who will live in the house as a principal residence, the seller pays the entire state transfer tax, and that tax drops to 0.25 percent. The seller also pays the recordation and local transfer taxes unless the contract expressly says the buyer will. Each buyer on the deed must sign a statement under oath for this rule to apply.

Tax or feeRate or ruleDefault payer
State transfer tax0.5 percent of considerationSplit equally unless contract says otherwise
State transfer tax, first-time buyer living in the home0.25 percentSeller
County or city transfer taxSet locallySplit equally, seller if first-time buyer
Recordation taxSet by countySplit equally, seller if first-time buyer

Read the offer for the exact allocation before you sign. We break the numbers down on the transfer tax and closing costs pages, and the Baltimore County clerk guide, Montgomery County clerk guide and Prince George's County clerk guide show how deeds are recorded in the three largest land records offices we cover.

sections.h2: What if my Maryland house has tenants?
sections.html:
A lease does not disappear because you decide to sell, and Maryland courts control how a tenant can be removed. Housing cases are heard by the District Court in the county where the property is located. A landlord cannot evict without first winning a judgment for possession and then getting a warrant of restitution.

  • For unpaid rent, the landlord must first give a written notice on form DC-CV-115 that states the rent owed and allows 10 days to pay.
  • After a judgment in a failure-to-pay-rent case, eviction cannot start until 7 business days have passed.
  • The landlord must request the warrant within 60 days of judgment in those cases.
  • The tenant must be told the eviction date at least 6 days ahead, and the sheriff or constable must be present.

Selling a rented house to a buyer who accepts it with tenants in place avoids a forced move. Read our guides on the eviction process, eviction notices and landlord and tenant rights for the full picture.

faqs.q: How many counties does Maryland have?
faqs.a: Maryland has 23 counties plus Baltimore, an independent city that works as a county equivalent. Tax, recording and probate offices follow those 24 jurisdictions.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Maryland?
faqs.a: Each county and Baltimore City keeps its own tax accounts. SDAT sets the assessment. Taxes are due July 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Maryland house while it is in foreclosure?
faqs.a: Often yes, if the sale covers the payoff. Owners can stop an auction by paying everything due up to one business day before it.

faqs.q: What happens to my house if it goes to tax sale?
faqs.a: The tax debt is sold, not the house. You still own it and can redeem until a court forecloses that right, though the cost rises over time.

faqs.q: Do I have to fix anything before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No. An as-is sale means the buyer takes the house in its current condition. Clear title and paid taxes still matter at closing.

faqs.q: How does a small estate work for an inherited home?
faqs.a: If probate assets are $50,000 or less, or $100,000 when a spouse is the only heir, the estate can open as a small estate through the Register of Wills. Larger estates use regular administration.

faqs.q: Who pays transfer tax when I sell?
faqs.a: By default buyer and seller split the state and local transfer taxes and recordation tax. If a first-time buyer will live there, the seller pays more of it. Check your contract.
